mappings.note: Unequal distances in equal times as the mark of non-uniform motion: the definition, not a calculation.
Metre per second as the SI unit of speed, the unit the chapter's calculations are expressed in.
Converts 3.6 km and 15 minutes into metres and seconds and divides: a speed calculation.
What a timetable must give before a train's speed can be worked out, namely distance and time: the inputs of the speed calculation.
Distance as speed times time, a rearrangement of the speed formula.
Applies that rearrangement to fifty kilometres an hour for two hours.
Time as distance over speed, the other rearrangement.
Applies it to 360 km at 90 km per hour.
Recognises total distance over total time as the average speed, which is what the formula actually yields for a real journey.
The correct way to write five hours as 5 h is a unit-writing convention, part of expressing measured quantities properly.
One second as the least count of a wall clock with a second hand: how finely time can be read off the instrument.
The millisecond as a thousandth of a second, a smaller unit for the same quantity.

Why sprint timing needs hundredths or thousandths of a second: the precision a measurement must have to serve its purpose. Not LO-109, because the answer is about the measurement, not a daily-life habit.
Over a fixed distance the shorter time means the greater speed: comparison through the speed relation.
Defines speed as distance covered in unit time, the quantity being measured throughout the chapter.
States the speed formula itself.
Reads two tables of ten-minute intervals and picks the train in uniform motion. The verdict is about the kind of motion, so LO-102 rather than LO-104, since no speed is computed.
Uniform motion is an idealisation because friction, air resistance and changing conditions keep altering the speed: the rarity traced to its causes.
Cruise control on an empty highway placed as the nearest thing to uniform linear motion: classifying a real case against the definition.
City traffic placed as non-uniform linear motion, the companion case.
Speed from 150 metres in ten seconds.
Converts 15 m/s into km/h, a unit conversion on the same quantity.
The Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar as the world's largest stone sundial: a piece of scientific heritage to appreciate, so LO-108 rather than device identification.
How the bottle water clock reads time, by marks made at one-minute intervals: explaining the working of the device the student built, which LO-107 covers.
Galileo and the swinging lamp: the discovery story behind the pendulum clock.
Huygens as the inventor of the pendulum clock, the next step in the same story.
Names the bob, the hanging mass of a pendulum: identification of a part.
Names the pendulum's swing as oscillatory and periodic motion, a kind of motion described.
One oscillation traced as O to A to B and back to O: the path of the motion described. The item that uses this to compute a period is on LO-104.

This row is internally inconsistent: the stem and options are the one-oscillation question (LO-102) while the printed answer and explanation are about the period depending on length and not mass (LO-101). Both halves are cited because each is honestly about the simple pendulum, and the mismatch is flagged as a defect.
The ghati as the unit the Ghatika-yantra measured, part of the historical account of Indian timekeeping.
A watch or stopwatch is needed to time the beats for a pulse rate, and LO-104 names pulse rate among the quantities to be measured.

Why repeated timings of the pendulum differ, namely reaction time and inconsistent release: sources of error in carrying out the investigation. Not LO-104, because the item is about the conduct of the experiment rather than the calculation.
A swing behaves like a pendulum, its period set by length and not by the rider's weight: the quantity tied to the variable that governs it.
Explains how the shadow of the gnomon moves across the dial to show time: the working of the device explained.
Describes an outflow or sinking-bowl water clock and how each marks time: again the working of a device.
One complete oscillation described from mean position out to both extremes and back.
Why the pendulum's motion counts as periodic: it repeats after a fixed interval.
Time many oscillations and divide by their number: the measurement procedure for the time period.
States that a longer pendulum has a longer period, which is the quantity related to what governs it.
The principle common to every clock, a process that repeats at regular intervals: the idea behind all the devices in the chapter.
The symbols s, min and h written correctly: conventions for recording measured time.
Determining the faster runner over equal distance by comparing times.
Speed from 120 km in two hours.
Writes the relation between distance, speed and time, the formula behind every calculation in the chapter.
